e-7133.knowledge_point: Restoring a Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
e-7133.problem:
Find a $2 \times 2$ matrix $C$ that has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=1$ and $\lambda_2=-4,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069457/assets/f478b4206f3a8bcc5c025fa0c58bb75430bcb1493c1d8470366864f7fb7ceb6e.png)
e-7133.worked_solution:
Since $\mathcal{B}= \{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $C,$ then $C$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $C=PDP^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $C,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order: 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069457/assets/1cf1ba5d93618341227836a110479ebfc258894f9d4f60ae4df1be682d7c74fc.png)

Let ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069457/assets/f1defa7b451fcd56632030e9c3663ad99646c5eabc98eb4e1c5b687687b9fdc4.png) Then

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2} & -\frac{5}{2} \\ -\frac{5}{2} & -\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

e-5502.knowledge_point: Raising a Matrix to a Large Power Using the Properties of Diagonalization
e-5502.worked_solution:
First,  notice that

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069457/assets/9c5de663d2cf109c4faaf839760b0afac6dcbf5ab533570100167727853cb74f.png)

So, we have been given the following diagonalization of $A\mathbin{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069457/assets/3f73ff47f00cf345f0ac0cffd41dc325faf00c9f1d1c0ffe4ad7228e83fef3fa.png)

Since $A=PDP^{-1},$ we can compute $A^k$ by using the formula 

$$
A^{k} = PD^{k}P^{-1}.
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{100} & =P{D}^{100}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{100}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{1}^{100} & 0 \\ 0 & {0}^{100}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

e-5503.knowledge_point: Finding the Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors of a Matrix Using the Properties of Diagonalization
e-5503.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2 \times 2$ matrix $E,$ given that 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069457/assets/3389ba82baf25977d7b8deb9609435dce5a543a863f7d8f98102b45d770b465b.png)
e-5503.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}3 & 6 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), left-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $E\mathbin{:}$ 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069457/assets/9dee992fa1cc903eb23299b52080a7ebba31ef550bb22c4938c45939e8541be4.png)

Therefore, $E$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $E$ are $\lambda_1=3$ and $\lambda_2=6$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P.$ Computing $P,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}P={[\begin{aligned}3 & 6 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{-3}[\begin{aligned}1 & -6 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} & 2 \\ \frac{1}{3} & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, the corresponding eigenvectors are

after.problem:
Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $F$ that has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -4\end{aligned}]
$$
after.worked_solution:
Since $B={{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $F,$ then $F$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $F=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $F,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
F={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}].$ Then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}-4 & -5 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -10 \\ 4 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-26 & -30 \\ 24 & 28\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

content.knowledge_point: Restoring a Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
content.problem:
Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $F$ that has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -4\end{aligned}]
$$
content.worked_solution:
Since $B={{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $F,$ then $F$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $F=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $F,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
F={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}].$ Then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}-4 & -5 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -10 \\ 4 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-26 & -30 \\ 24 & 28\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $S$ that has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
Since $B={{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $S,$ then $S$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $S=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $S,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
S={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}].$ Then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}18 & 1 \\ 15 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}13 & -12 \\ 10 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Restoring a Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
content.problem:
Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $S$ that has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
Since $B={{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $S,$ then $S$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $S=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $S,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
S={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}].$ Then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}18 & 1 \\ 15 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}13 & -12 \\ 10 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can write $A=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $A$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
A={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}].$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain,

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 15 \\ 4 & 10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ -2 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Restoring a Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
content.problem:
Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ that has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=5,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
Since $B={{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $A$, then  $A$ must be diagonalizable. 

So, we can write $A=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $A$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
A={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}].$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain,

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 15 \\ 4 & 10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ -2 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $E$ that has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=6,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
Since $B={{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $E,$ then $E$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $E=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $E,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
E={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 4 & 4\end{aligned}].$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 4 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}E & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 4 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}](\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}12 & 12 \\ 16 & 24\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ -8 & 10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Restoring a Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
content.problem:
Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $E$ that has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=6,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
Since $B={{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $E,$ then $E$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $E=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $E,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
E={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 4 & 4\end{aligned}].$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 4 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}E & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 4 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}](\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}12 & 12 \\ 16 & 24\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ -8 & 10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}10 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}](-\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}10 & 15 \\ 20 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ -2 & 11\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Restoring a Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
content.problem:
Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $C$ that has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=10$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=5,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
Since $B={{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $C,$ then $C$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $C=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $C,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
C={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}10 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}](-\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}10 & 15 \\ 20 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ -2 & 11\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 6
after.worked_solution:
We have been given the following diagonalization of $A.$

$$
A={{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

So, since $A=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${A}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{A}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the inverse of the matrix $P.$ We get

$$
{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{-2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]=-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{97} & =P{D}^{97}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{97}{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}(-1)^{97} & 0 \\ 0 & {1}^{97}\end{aligned}](-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Raising a Matrix to a Large Power Using the Properties of Diagonalization
content.worked_solution:
We have been given the following diagonalization of $A.$

$$
A={{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

So, since $A=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${A}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{A}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the inverse of the matrix $P.$ We get

$$
{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{-2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]=-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{97} & =P{D}^{97}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{97}{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}(-1)^{97} & 0 \\ 0 & {1}^{97}\end{aligned}](-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Since A=PDP^{-1}, A^{69}=PD^{69}P^{-1}. Because 69 is odd, D^{69}=diag(1,-1). With P^{-1}=[[-1/2,-1/6],[0,-1/6]], multiplication gives A^{69}=[[1,2/3],[0,-1]], option b.

after.name: Question 7
after.worked_solution:
We have been given the following diagonalization of $A.$

$$
A={{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

So, since $A=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${A}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{A}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the inverse of the matrix $P.$ We get

$$
{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}-6 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{69} & =P{D}^{69}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{69}{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{1}^{69} & 0 \\ 0 & (-1)^{69}\end{aligned}](\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}-6 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-6 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-6 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & \frac{2}{3} \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].

So, we have been given the following diagonalization of $G:$

$$
G={{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Since $G=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${G}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{G}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}{G}^{10} & =P{D}^{10}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]}^{10}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{2}^{10} & 0 \\ 0 & (-2)^{10}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1024 & 0 \\ 0 & 1024\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1024 & 0 \\ 1024 & 1024\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1024 & 0 \\ 0 & 1024\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

EXPLANATION

First, notice that

[−1011]−1=[−1011].

So, we have been given the following diagonalization of G:

G=[−1011]⏟P[200−2]⏟D[−1011]−1⏟P−1

Since G=PDP−1, we can compute Gk by using the formula Gk=PDkP−1.

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

G10=PD10P−1=[−1011][200−2]10[−1011]=[−1011][21000(−2)10][−1011]=[−1011][1024001024][−1011]=[−1024010241024][−1011]=[1024001024].

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option a. Since P^{-1}=P and D^{10}=diag(2^{10},(-2)^{10})=1024I, G^{10}=P(1024I)P^{-1}=1024I. The incorrect submission selected b.

content.knowledge_point: Raising a Matrix to a Large Power Using the Properties of Diagonalization
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that

$$
{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have been given the following diagonalization of $G:$

$$
G={{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Since $G=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${G}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{G}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}{G}^{10} & =P{D}^{10}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]}^{10}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{2}^{10} & 0 \\ 0 & (-2)^{10}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1024 & 0 \\ 0 & 1024\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1024 & 0 \\ 1024 & 1024\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1024 & 0 \\ 0 & 1024\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

Find C36, where C=[3−1−32][31800336][231311].

a
[129−24−3]
b
[63−12−9]
c
[156−12−3]
d
[159−21−6]
e
[126−18−21]
Submit

decision.explanation: The final matrix is P^{-1}, so C^{36}=PD^{36}P^{-1}. Since (3^{1/18})^{36}=9 and (3^{1/36})^{36}=3, multiplying P diag(9,3) P^{-1} gives [[15,6],[-12,-3]], option c.

after.name: Question 9
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that

$$
{[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have been given the following diagonalization of $C:$

$$
C={{[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}\sqrt[18]{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[36]{3}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Since $C=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${C}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{C}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{36} & =P{D}^{36}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}\sqrt[18]{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[36]{3}\end{aligned}]}^{36}(\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}(\sqrt[18]{3})^{36} & 0 \\ 0 & (\sqrt[36]{3})^{36}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{3}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & {3}^{1}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}27 & -3 \\ -27 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}15 & 6 \\ -12 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

Find C36, where C=[3−1−32][31800336][231311].

a
[129−24−3]
b
[63−12−9]
c
[156−12−3]
d
[159−21−6]
e
[126−18−21]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that

[3−1−32]−1=[231311]=13[2133].

So, we have been given the following diagonalization of C:

C=[3−1−32]⏟P[31800336]⏟D[3−1−32]−1⏟P−1

Since C=PDP−1, we can compute Ck by using the formula Ck=PDkP−1.

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

C36=PD36P−1=[3−1−32][31800336]36(13[2133])=13[3−1−32][(318)3600(336)36][2133]=13[3−1−32][320031][2133]=13[3−1−32][9003][2133]=13[27−3−276][2133]=[156−12−3]

content.knowledge_point: Raising a Matrix to a Large Power Using the Properties of Diagonalization
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that

$$
{[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have been given the following diagonalization of $C:$

$$
C={{[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}\sqrt[18]{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[36]{3}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Since $C=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${C}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{C}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{36} & =P{D}^{36}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}\sqrt[18]{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[36]{3}\end{aligned}]}^{36}(\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}(\sqrt[18]{3})^{36} & 0 \\ 0 & (\sqrt[36]{3})^{36}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{3}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & {3}^{1}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}27 & -3 \\ -27 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}15 & 6 \\ -12 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Using M^{16}=PD^{16}P^{-1}, the diagonal entries become 2^{16/8}=4 and 2^{16/4}=16. Since P^{-1}=[[2,-3],[-1,2]], multiplication gives M^{16}=[[-32,72],[-24,52]], option a.

after.name: Question 10
after.worked_solution:
We have been given the following diagonalization of $M.$

$$
M={{[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}\sqrt[8]{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[4]{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

So, since $M=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${M}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{M}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the inverse of the matrix $P.$ We get

$$
{[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}^{16} & =P{D}^{16}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}\sqrt[8]{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[4]{2}\end{aligned}]}^{16}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}(\sqrt[8]{2})^{16} & 0 \\ 0 & (\sqrt[4]{2})^{16}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{4}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 16\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 48 \\ 4 & 32\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-32 & 72 \\ -24 & 52\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Find M16, where M=[2312][280024][2312]−1.

a
[−3272−2452]
b
[24−3−112]
c
[−32−1212−13]
d
[12481232]
e
[120016]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We have been given the following diagonalization of M.

M=[2312]⏟P[280024]⏟D[2312]−1⏟P−1

So, since M=PDP−1, we can compute Mk by using the formula Mk=PDkP−1.

First, we find the inverse of the matrix P. We get [2312]−1=11[2−3−12]=[2−3−12].

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

M16=PD16P−1=[2312][280024]16[2−3−12]=[2312][(28)1600(24)16][2−3−12]=[2312][220024][2−3−12]=[2312][40016][2−3−12]=[848432][2−3−12]=[−3272−2452]

content.knowledge_point: Raising a Matrix to a Large Power Using the Properties of Diagonalization
content.worked_solution:
We have been given the following diagonalization of $M.$

$$
M={{[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}\sqrt[8]{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[4]{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

So, since $M=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${M}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{M}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the inverse of the matrix $P.$ We get

$$
{[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}^{16} & =P{D}^{16}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}\sqrt[8]{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[4]{2}\end{aligned}]}^{16}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}(\sqrt[8]{2})^{16} & 0 \\ 0 & (\sqrt[4]{2})^{16}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{4}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 16\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 48 \\ 4 & 32\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-32 & 72 \\ -24 & 52\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11
?

Find the eigenvectors of the 2×2 matrix L given that L[322−3]=[322−3][−4004].

a
[12] and [2−1]
b
[32] and [2−3]
c
[−40] and [04]
d
[3−2] and [23]
e
[3−2] and [−2−3]
Submit

decision.explanation: Comparing columns in LP=PD gives L(3,2)=-4(3,2) and L(2,-3)=4(2,-3). Thus the columns (3,2) and (2,-3) are eigenvectors, as displayed in option b. Any nonzero scalar multiples are also eigenvectors.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $L$ given that 

$$
L[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), right-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $L:$

$$
L={{[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $L$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $L$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=4$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P:$
$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]$

Question 11
?

Find the eigenvectors of the 2×2 matrix L given that L[322−3]=[322−3][−4004].

a
[12] and [2−1]
b
[32] and [2−3]
c
[−40] and [04]
d
[3−2] and [23]
e
[3−2] and [−2−3]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that the matrix [322−3] appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), right-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for L: L=[322−3]⏟P[−4004]⏟D[322−3]−1⏟P−1

Therefore, L is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of L are λ1=−4 and λ2=4 and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix P: v1=[32] and v2=[2−3]

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors of a Matrix Using the Properties of Diagonalization
content.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $L$ given that 

$$
L[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), right-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $L:$

$$
L={{[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $L$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $L$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=4$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P:$
$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]$

Question 12
?

Find the eigenvectors of the 2×2 matrix T given that [7532]T=[500−4][7532].

a
[−23] and [5−7]
b
[−43] and [5−1]
c
[−42] and [6−7]
d
[−28] and [7−1]
e
[−33] and [5−5]
Submit

decision.explanation: Writing Q=[[7,5],[3,2]], the equation QT=DQ gives T=Q^{-1}DQ. Since Q^{-1}=[[-2,5],[3,-7]], its columns (-2,3) and (5,-7) are eigenvectors for eigenvalues 5 and -4, respectively. Nonzero scalar multiples are also eigenvectors.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $T$ given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]T=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), left-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $T:$

$$
T={{{[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $T$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $T$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-4$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P.$ Computing $P,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}P={[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ -3 & 7\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 5 \\ 3 & -7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, the corresponding eigenvectors are: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -7\end{aligned}]$

Question 12
?

Find the eigenvectors of the 2×2 matrix T given that [7532]T=[500−4][7532].

a
[−23] and [5−7]
b
[−43] and [5−1]
c
[−42] and [6−7]
d
[−28] and [7−1]
e
[−33] and [5−5]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Notice that the matrix [7532] appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), left-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for T:

T=[7532]−1⏟P[500−4]⏟D[7532]⏟P−1

Therefore, T is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of T are λ1=5 and λ2=−4 and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix P. Computing P, we obtain

P=[7532]−1=1−1[2−5−37]=[−253−7].

In conclusion, the corresponding eigenvectors are:

v1=[−23] and v2=[5−7]

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option a. From QT=DQ, T=Q^{-1}DQ, and Q^{-1}=[[-2,5],[3,-7]]. Its columns (-2,3) and (5,-7) are eigenvectors for eigenvalues 5 and -4, respectively; nonzero scalar multiples also qualify. The incorrect submission selected c.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors of a Matrix Using the Properties of Diagonalization
content.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $T$ given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]T=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), left-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $T:$

$$
T={{{[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $T$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $T$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-4$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P.$ Computing $P,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}P={[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ -3 & 7\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 5 \\ 3 & -7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, the corresponding eigenvectors are: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -7\end{aligned}]$

Question 13
?

Find the eigenvectors of the 2×2 matrix E given that [1154]E=[3002][1154].

a
[4−5] and [−21]
b
[−41] and [5−4]
c
[−54] and [1−1]
d
[15] and [14]
e
[−45] and [1−1]
Submit

decision.explanation: Let Q=[[1,1],[5,4]]. From QE=DQ, E=Q^{-1}DQ. Since Q^{-1}=[[-4,1],[5,-1]], its columns (-4,5) and (1,-1) are eigenvectors for eigenvalues 3 and 2, respectively. Nonzero scalar multiples are also eigenvectors.

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $E$ given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 5 & 4\end{aligned}]E=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 5 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 5 & 4\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), left-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $E:$

$$
E={{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 5 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 5 & 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $E$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $E$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P.$ Computing $P,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}P={[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 5 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ -5 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 1 \\ 5 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, the corresponding eigenvectors are: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$

Question 13
?

Find the eigenvectors of the 2×2 matrix E given that [1154]E=[3002][1154].

a
[4−5] and [−21]
b
[−41] and [5−4]
c
[−54] and [1−1]
d
[15] and [14]
e
[−45] and [1−1]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that the matrix [1154] appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), left-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for E:

E=[1154]−1⏟P[3002]⏟D[1154]⏟P−1

Therefore, E is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of E are λ1=3 and λ2=2 and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix P. Computing P, we obtain

P=[1154]−1=1−1[4−1−51]=[−415−1].

In conclusion, the corresponding eigenvectors are:

v1=[−45] and v2=[1−1]

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors of a Matrix Using the Properties of Diagonalization
content.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $E$ given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 5 & 4\end{aligned}]E=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 5 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 5 & 4\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), left-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $E:$

$$
E={{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 5 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 5 & 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $E$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $E$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P.$ Computing $P,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}P={[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 5 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ -5 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 1 \\ 5 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, the corresponding eigenvectors are: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$

Question 14
?

Find the eigenvectors of the 2×2 matrix B given that B[3411]=[3411][0002].

a
[4−1] and [31]
b
[01] and [32]
c
[−14] and [1−3]
d
[−13] and [−14]
e
[31] and [41]
Submit

decision.explanation: Comparing columns in BP=PD gives B(3,1)=0(3,1) and B(4,1)=2(4,1). Thus (3,1) and (4,1) are eigenvectors for eigenvalues 0 and 2, respectively. Any nonzero scalar multiples are also eigenvectors.

after.name: Question 14
after.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $B$ given that 

$$
B[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), right-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $B:$ 

$$
B={{[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore $B$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P:$
$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

a
[4−1] and [31]
b
[01] and [32]

EXPLANATION

Notice that the matrix [3411] appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), right-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for B: B=[3411]⏟P[0002]⏟D[3411]−1⏟P−1

Therefore B is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of B are λ1=0 and λ2=2 and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix P: v1=[31] and v2=[41].

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors of a Matrix Using the Properties of Diagonalization
content.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $B$ given that 

$$
B[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), right-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $B:$ 

$$
B={{[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore $B$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P:$
$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

after.name: Question 15
after.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $B$ given that 

$$
B[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), right-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $B:$

$$
B={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $B$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P:$

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$
